items.title: Howard Alden interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: And we play together quite often both in a duo situation, which is a lot of fun

ctx.x: Who are some of your favorite compatriots to work with these days?

Well let’s see, you just talked to one of them, Ken Peplowski. We’ve known each other almost fifteen years, probably about twelve or thirteen years. And we play together quite often both in a duo situation, which is a lot of fun, and next week we’re working a trio with Michael Moore and larger groups too, quartets and stuff like that. He’s great too

because we really do have like a musical conversation when we play. Either one of us can go any way at any time and the other person is fearless enough to attempt to follow or not, as the choice may be. And he’s got the flexibility on his instruments to pull off just about anything he thinks of. So I love playing with Ken. And Bucky I enjoy playing with. There’s a lot of different things. items.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And Howard and I love playing together. We’ve had a long musical relationship and we’ve done some duo records.

ctx.x: Now this section here, it’s almost like you guys are both soloing at the same time.

We are. I like to do that a lot. And Howard and I love playing together. We’ve had a long musical relationship and we’ve done some duo records. And it’s fun because he’s not just a rhythm guitarist. He is great in a quintet because he can function as another horn, and I love to do that when I’m using my own musicians, collective improvisation, in a more modern setting like that. It was done years ago in New Orleans jazz, in traditional jazz, so why can’t it be done now? The trick is to not fill up every available…
Did you ever have the experience where you felt you had to play much, much harder because the rhythm section wasn’t good?
